html:
The Orkhon inscriptions are two stone memorials in the Orkhon Valley of Mongolia, set up in 732 and 735. They are the oldest known long texts in a Turkic language.

They honour two brothers who led the Second Turkic Khaganate, one of the Türk Khaganates: the prince Kul Tigin, who died in 731, and his brother the ruler Bilge Khagan, who died in 734. They are written in the Old Turkic script, whose angular letters look like runes, with a Chinese text on one side.

The texts speak in the khagan's voice. They tell the history of the Turks, praise the dead, and warn the people. The Chinese, they say, give sweet words and soft silks to lure Turks away from their homeland; those who stay in the forest of Ötüken will keep their power.

Russian explorers found the stones in 1889. In 1893 the Danish scholar Vilhelm Thomsen deciphered the script. Today Turks and Kazakhs see them as the start of their written history. The valley, which later held the Mongol capital Karakorum, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
sum: The Orkhon inscriptions are two stone memorials in the Orkhon Valley of Mongolia, set up in 732 and 735. They are the oldest known long texts in a Turkic language.
